primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'faith' primarily denotes trusting belief in and personal reliance upon God and, specifically, upon Jesus Christ for salvation. It is classically defined as confident assurance in what is hoped for and conviction about unseen realities, and it functions as the instrumental means by which a person is justified and receives God's grace (trust, not mere intellectual agreement).
primary_basis: Hebrews 11:1 ('faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen')
Hebrews 11:6 ('without faith it is impossible to please God')
Ephesians 2:8-9 ('by grace you have been saved through faith')
Romans 1:17 / Habakkuk 2:4 ('the righteous shall live by faith')
Romans 4:3 / Genesis 15:6 (Abraham 'believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness')
Romans 5:1 ('justified by faith, we have peace with God')
Galatians 2:16 (justified by faith in Christ, not works of the law)
Romans 10:9-10 (believing in the heart unto salvation)
John 3:16 (whoever believes in him has eternal life)
Mark 11:22-24 (faith in God expressed in prayer)

alternatives.meaning: Faith as faithfulness or covenant fidelity — steadfast loyalty and obedience rather than (or in addition to) inward trust; includes the scholarly 'pistis Christou' debate over whether Paul means 'faith in Christ' or 'the faithfulness of Christ' (e.g., Richard Hays, N.T. Wright).
'The faith' as a fixed body of doctrine or the objective content of Christian belief (fides quae creditur) — the deposit of apostolic teaching to be guarded and defended.
basis: Jude 3 ('contend for the faith once for all delivered to the saints')
1 Timothy 4:1 ('some will depart from the faith')

alternatives.meaning: Faith as inseparable from works — living faith necessarily produces obedience and love, so faith without works is dead; emphasized in Catholic, Orthodox, and many Protestant readings ('faith working through love').
Faith as a sovereign gift of God rather than an autonomous human act — the Reformed/Calvinist emphasis that even the believing itself is divinely granted.
basis: Ephesians 2:8-9 ('and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God')
Romans 12:3 ('the measure of faith God has assigned')

alternatives.meaning: Faith as effective spiritual power or 'force' that produces miracles, healing, or material results when spoken and acted upon — characteristic of Pentecostal/charismatic and especially Word of Faith teaching.
basis: Matthew 9:22 ('your faith has made you well')

alternatives.meaning: Faith as one of the spiritual gifts — a special charism of extraordinary trust given to some believers, distinct from saving faith common to all.
basis: 1 Corinthians 12:9 ('to another faith by the same Spirit')
1 Corinthians 13:2 ('faith so as to move mountains')

alternatives.meaning: Faith reduced to intellectual assent (assensus) to propositions — historically distinguished (and generally rejected as insufficient) by theologians who separate notitia, assensus, and fiducia; James's 'even the demons believe' is cited against it.

notes: 'Faith' is less a symbol than a central theological concept, but its consensus meaning is well settled: trusting reliance on God/Christ as the instrument of justification (Hebrews 11:1; Ephesians 2:8; Romans 4-5). The main live disputes are not about this core meaning but about its scope and mechanics: faith vs. faithfulness (translation of pistis and the pistis Christou debate), the relationship of faith to works (Catholic-Protestant divide, largely narrowed by ecumenical statements such as the 1999 Joint Declaration on Justification), whether faith is itself God's gift, and Word of Faith claims that treat faith as a quasi-force. The classical threefold analysis (notitia/knowledge, assensus/assent, fiducia/trust) is widely used across traditions to hold these strands together.
